Title: Why the Harness Matters: Early Lessons From the Evo Code Scanning Agent Preview
Context: It found 13% of the known vulnerabilities, and only about three in five of its first attempts produced a usable result
Full Text:
Evo Code Scanning Agent is in experimental preview with select Snyk customers. We’re building it to bring together AI reasoning, specialized models, deterministic analysis, security knowledge, and a context layer that draws on insights from across Snyk’s products to find vulnerabilities that are difficult to detect with any one approach alone. There’s a lot that goes into that system; we’re taking a closer look at one of its building blocks, the security harness that guides how an AI model explores code, investigates potential vulnerabilities, and reports findings.

To see what the harness contributes on its own, we paired it with the same off-the-shelf models used by Claude Security and Codex Security. At the same compute budget, Evo Code Scanning Agent found more known vulnerabilities than either, though both tools achieved higher precision. These are early results, and the agent is still evolving. If you’re a Snyk customer and want to try it, join the preview / talk to your Snyk account team.

For this test, we ran two pairs, each on a single model:

Evo Code Scanning Agent and Claude Security, both on Claude Sonnet 5.5

Evo Code Scanning Agent and Codex Security in deep mode, both on GPT-6.1 Sol

Every scanner ran against the same 14 applications, at least three times per app, and was scored against 1,426 known vulnerabilities.

Share of known vulnerabilities found at the same compute budget, averaged over 14 applications.

More findings at the same compute budget

The completeness of an AI scanner’s results depends on the compute budget it’s given. To compare like with like, we gave Evo Code Scanning Agent the same compute budget as each lab tool, on average across the 14 applications. Against Claude Security, it found 57% of the known vulnerabilities, versus 32%. Against Codex Security, it found 66%, versus 43%. It found more than the respective lab tool on every one of the 14 applications.

Finding more vulnerabilities, understanding their impact

Both lab tools were more precise than Evo Code Scanning Agent. Claude Security checks each candidate with a verification panel that looks at reachability, defenses and impact, and Codex Security’s deep mode runs review rounds before it reports. We’re currently improving the precision of our harness, and refining the ground truths we use in measurement.

At equal compute, Evo Code Scanning Agent found more known vulnerabilities than either lab tool, with different precision tradeoffs across the two models. On GPT-6.1 Sol, it found 66% of the known vulnerabilities to Codex Security’s 43%, at 90% precision versus 97.5%. On Claude Sonnet 5.5, it found 57% to Claude Security’s 32%, with a larger precision gap: 65% versus 94%. We’re deliberately prioritizing broader vulnerability discovery while continuing to improve precision.

We’re also exploring how context from across Snyk’s products can help teams understand each finding’s significance, including whether weaknesses that appear less urgent on their own could combine into a more serious attack. As AI changes how attackers investigate and connect vulnerabilities, the broader context will become increasingly valuable.

Same model, different findings

Holding the model fixed makes the harness effect easy to see. At the same compute budget on Claude Sonnet 5.5, Evo Code Scanning Agent found about three in four of the vulnerabilities Claude Security found, plus roughly 470 more across the 14 applications. On GPT-6.1 Sol, it found about six in seven of what Codex Security deep found, plus roughly 420 more. Each lab tool still found vulnerabilities Evo Code Scanning Agent missed: 111 for Claude Security and 84 for Codex Security deep.

Known vulnerabilities found by each tool on Claude Sonnet 5.5 at the same compute budget, averaged over runs and summed across 14 applications. The 314 found by both count toward each tool’s total, so together the two found 893 of the 1,426. Neither found the other 533.

Known vulnerabilities found by each tool on GPT-6.1 Sol at the same compute budget, averaged over runs and summed across 14 applications. The 478 found by both count toward each tool’s total, so together the two found 982 of the 1,426. Neither found the other 444.

Because the model was identical within each pair, the difference comes from everything around it: how the harness plans the work, splits up the code, investigates candidates, and decides what to keep.

A general-purpose coding agent isn’t enough

For a baseline, we ran OpenHands, a widely used open source coding agent, with the open-weights GLM-5.3 model and a single prompt asking for a list of security findings. It found 13% of the known vulnerabilities, and only about three in five of its first attempts produced a usable result. This comparison changes both the model and the harness, so it doesn’t isolate either one. It does establish a starting point: a capable coding agent with a reasonable prompt finds a fraction of what the purpose-built tools found.

Scope and limits of these results

These are early results from a benchmark Snyk built and ran internally. The 14 applications combine open source projects with purpose-built benchmark apps, and we report the results in aggregate only. Evo Code Scanning Agent is in Experimental Preview and still evolving, and this test measured one part of it, the AI harness, on its own.

No tool in the test found every known vulnerability. The strongest result, 66% on GPT-6.1 Sol, still left about a third unfound. For that reason, we see AI security agents as one layer of an AppSec program. They work alongside SAST, SCA and code review, and each of those catches issues the others can miss.

Methodology

All results come from Snyk’s internal benchmark of 14 applications, a mix of open source projects and purpose-built benchmark apps, scored against 1,426 known vulnerabilities. Each scanner scanned the same source tree for each application at least three times, and partial runs count as runs.

How we measured

Recall: the share of an application’s known vulnerabilities a result finds, averaged over the 14 applications. Two reports of the same vulnerability count once.

Equal compute: We let Evo Code Scanning Agent run until its compute spend reached, without exceeding, the average cost of one scan by the same-model lab tool. Lab tools are scored on their average scan.

Precision: distinct vulnerabilities found ÷ (distinct vulnerabilities found + distinct false positives), measured on the same results as recall at the same compute budget. Evo Code Scanning Agent’s figure on Claude Sonnet 5.5 is a lower bound, because some duplicate false positives couldn’t be merged.

How we scored findings

Labels: two independent AI reviewers judged every finding against the known vulnerabilities, with a third deciding when they disagreed. No finding was reviewed by a human. Findings the reviewers couldn’t decide do not count in either recall or precision.

Answer key: the 1,426 known vulnerabilities include every vulnerability confirmed from any scanner’s findings, and every scan was rechecked against every entry.

Beyond the harness

Holding the model constant showed how much the harness alone shapes what an AI scanner finds. The harness is one building block of Evo Code Scanning Agent, and upcoming posts will cover the others: how we’re making findings consistent from one run to the next, how static analysis and AI analysis work together, how we plan to train models for security, and how context from across Snyk’s products helps teams understand and prioritize what the agent finds.

Title: Say Yes To MCP, Safely A Guide For Governing AI Coding Agents With Evo ADS
Context: When we announced that MCP Governance is generally available in Evo Agentic Development Security (ADS), the most common follow-up was practical: "Great
Full Text:
When we announced that MCP Governance is generally available in Evo Agentic Development Security (ADS), the most common follow-up was practical: "Great. Where do I start on Monday?"

It’s a fair question; across 10,000 developer environments, Snyk found 4,524 unique MCP servers in active use, and 1 in 12 developers with an MCP server installed had a confirmed high or critical finding. Most of those servers were added in seconds, by a developer trying to get their agent to do something useful, with no review behind them.

Here’s our answer: four steps can take you from a first inventory to policies that block only the servers that are risky. Evo ADS now provides a risk score for MCP servers so you can govern by risk, with or without an allowlist, instead of reviewing every server by hand or blocking broadly and slowing developers down. Everything runs on the endpoint where agents already work, through lightweight hooks with no proxy in the way. Discover what's there, define what's acceptable, observe what your policy catches, and enforce with confidence.

Step 1: Discover what’s already running

MCP servers don't pass through CI or dependency reviews. A developer edits one config file, and their agent has a new set of tools. So the first step is to find out what’s already there. You can’t govern what you can’t see, so Evo ADS gives you two views:

MCP servers on developer machines: Deploy the Evo ADS installer across your fleet. It surfaces the MCP servers agents are actually connecting to, including one-off local installs that never touched a repo.

MCP servers in code repositories: Evo AI-SPM, set up through Snyk's SCM integration, finds MCP servers referenced in your code.

Together, these answer two different questions: what is configured in code, and what is running on laptops. Both land within the Evo UI, in Inventory → MCP servers.

You can also use the Evo MCP Server to access this data using your own agentic workflow. This gives you one view of your MCP estate, with nothing blocked and no disruption to developers. With this one step, you can now answer a question most security teams can’t: what are our agents connected to?

Step 2: Define what "acceptable" means

Deciding whether server number 47 is okay shouldn't take a Slack thread and a web search. Evo ADS puts the evidence next to every server, so you can approve or reject faster, with confidence.

Read the inventory

A high-risk, widely installed, unofficial server is a very different problem from a high-risk one on a single machine. Each row answers the questions you’d otherwise chase down by hand: who built this server, where it’s installed, whether anyone approved it, and how risky it is:

Server: name, origin (for example, NPM), transport (SSE or STDIO), and whether it is local.

Vendor origin: whether the server is Official. Unknown is a signal too.

Source: how many times it appears in code, on machines, and at runtime.

Allowlist status: Allowed or not allowed.

Risk score: one unified score per server, sortable and filterable.

Issues by severity: critical, high, medium, and low counts.

Sort by risk score, then scan across.

Open the Risk profile

Click a server for the detail view. The header adds authentication methods, and three cards show where it lives: declared in code, on how many machines and when last scanned, and how often agents called it in the last seven days.

Then open the Risk profile tab. This is the tab that replaces the Slack thread and the web search.

In one server we examined, Evo found tool descriptions containing ‘ignore previous instructions’ in 8 of 12 instances. That’s prompt injection you’d only catch by reading every tool description yourself.

Scores run from 0 to 1000:

Low (0 to 249)

Medium (250 to 499)

High (500 to 749)

Critical (750 to 1000)

The tab breaks the score into attributes such as prompt injection in tool description, destructive capabilities, and untrusted content, each scored out of 1000. Expand one for a description and a "Why this risk?" explanation with evidence.

This server was already on the allowlist. Someone approved it, and it still scores 931, firmly Critical. An allowlist records a decision made at one point in time; the risk score tells you when that decision needs another look. You can move it to “Not allowed” from this page, or block it at runtime.

How servers get scored

The MCP risk score combines three signals: server behavior (the instructions and tool descriptions it sends to agents), trust (the reputation of its URLs and the identity of its maintainers), and, for local servers with source available, implementation, maintenance, and dependencies. One limitation is that Evo can't confidently identify servers without a signature. That is fewer than 20% of servers, and they don't get a score. Plan for them in your review process.

Set your baseline

The allowlist is your record of which MCP servers you have approved. Each server has a toggle: approved or not. Flip it, and the decision appears in the Allowlist status column of the inventory (Allowed or Not allowed), so everyone viewing the inventory sees the same state. View the allowlist in a server's detail view to see the full list.

Start with what you already trust; you don't need to build it from scratch. Seed it from an existing inventory, a curated list, or the servers Evo ADS has already discovered. Toggle servers manually in the inventory, or just ask Evo in the chat.

For each candidate, check what you learned above: the score band, whether the vendor is Official, how it authenticates, and, for anything High or Critical, the "Why this risk?" evidence. A low-scoring, official, authenticated server is an easy yes. A critical one deserves a reason before you approve it, and a rejection is a perfectly good answer.

Remember, the allowlist records decisions. It doesn't block anything by itself. Policies act on those decisions, which is where the next steps come in.

Step 3: Observe before you block

Turning on blocking on day one breaks developer workflows you haven’t seen yet. Monitor mode shows you exactly what your policy would block before it blocks anything. Create your first policy from the Monitor not allowed MCP servers template on the Policy page (Policies → Issues → Create policy). It raises each risky server as an issue to review, without blocking anything. This way, developers and agents keep working, and you get a running list of everything your policy would catch.

Then work that list in Inventory → MCP servers, using the row and Risk profile you learned in Step 2. For each flagged server, check the score, whether it is official and how it authenticates, and which attributes drove the score. Then decide: approve it onto the allowlist, or reject it. Do this for a week or two and watch for patterns. A server that shows up once is a curiosity, but a server that shows up across fifty machines is a decision you need to make deliberately.

By the end of the second week, you have a policy that reflects your risk appetite, tested against your real estate, with your security and developers having seen it working before it ever stops them.

Step 4: Enforce, starting with what's risky

Once you trust what the policy catches, switch on enforcement. The Block not allowed MCP servers policy template (Policies → Policies → Create policy) prevents coding agents from calling servers that are not on your allowlist and are rated high or critical risk at runtime on the endpoint. If the template doesn't match your appetite, use Start from scratch and build a custom policy on your own criteria.

The policy blocks a server only when it’s both off your allowlist and rated High or Critical. Everything else keeps running in log mode, so a low-risk server that nobody has approved yet won’t stop a developer, and you still keep an audit trail. Additionally, enforcement happens locally at runtime on the developer’s machine, through lightweight hooks that sit alongside the agent, rather than as a proxy or gateway in its path. You set policy once, centrally. Hooks enforce it on each machine at the moment the agent calls the server, whether that’s Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or GitHub Copilot.

Say yes to MCP, with control

So, Monday you deploy the installer and connect your SCM; by Friday, you have an inventory and a seeded allowlist. With Evo ADS, you can say yes to MCP and still know what your agents connect to, decide quickly, and block what's risky. This is the first use case under Govern Agent Behavior, and we're just getting started: over the rest of the year, the same discover, classify, and enforce model extends to agent skills, sensitive data access, prompt injection protection, and secret exposure.

Title: Snyk Named a Leader in The Forrester Wave™: Agentic Development Security Tools, Q4 2026
Context: AI makes it cheap to chain several of those minor issues into a critical exploit path, so the backlog now functions as an attack surface rather than deferred cleanup
Full Text:
We're proud to share that Snyk has been named a Leader in The Forrester Wave™: Agentic Development Security Tools, Q4 2026. Snyk received the highest score in the Strategy category, along with the highest scores possible in these criteria:

Strategy: Vision, Roadmap, and Partner Ecosystem

Current offering: AI dynamic testing, AI coding guardrails, autonomous proprietary code remediation, and developer experience

Software development changed who does the work

For two decades, software development moved at a human pace where developers wrote code, peers reviewed it, and security teams tested it on a schedule. AI coding assistants compressed that cycle, and coding agents are now changing who does the work. Forrester frames the shift: "AI coding agents are changing how software is built, moving from developer assistants to active participants in development workflows."

Adoption has moved well past the pilot stage. In the Stack Overflow 2026 Developer Survey, 66% of developers who use AI work in coding agents, and 73% of those using AI coding assistants or agents use them daily. As a result, the developer's role is shifting from writing every line to orchestrating the agents that write it.

Each of those agents brings its own supply chain; it installs packages, connects to MCP servers, loads skills, and invokes tools the security team may never have reviewed. Because it can also run commands, edit files, and access sensitive data, its actions need to be governed as much as its code needs to be tested. In our view, security models built to scan code after it is written were not designed to govern the systems creating it.

Attackers are moving at machine speed too

In 2025, Anthropic's threat intelligence team disrupted an espionage campaign in which AI carried out an estimated 80 to 90% of tactical operations, with humans in a supervisory role. The CrowdStrike 2026 Global Threat Report puts average eCrime breakout time, from initial access to lateral movement, at 29 minutes, with the fastest observed case at 27 seconds.

Those timelines change how teams should think about their vulnerability backlog. Pull request queues, ticket triage, and quarterly pentests were designed around attackers who moved slower than the fix. Most backlogs consist of low- and medium-severity findings, deprioritized one at a time. AI makes it cheap to chain several of those minor issues into a critical exploit path, so the backlog now functions as an attack surface rather than deferred cleanup.

The pressure is also building inside the codebase; Snyk’s product data shows new critical and high-severity issues detected grew 10x in the past year, and roughly eight new issues are introduced for every one remediated. When risk is created faster than it is fixed, the answer is a different operating model: security agents that fix continuously, guardrails inside the agent workflow, and adversarial testing that proves controls hold

AI applications are reaching production faster than governance

Teams are shipping AI applications and agents into production faster than governance processes can keep pace with. Many security leaders are still working to answer basic questions about their AI estate:

Which models, agents, and MCP servers are running, and what data can they reach?

Which skills were pulled from public registries, and who approved them?

Could you audit what a given agent did last week?

This is shadow AI at enterprise scale. Its risks, such as prompt injection, excessive agency, and data leakage, are behavioral: they live in an agent’s decisions as well as its code, which is why code scanning alone can’t surface them. Model choice is part of that risk. In Snyk’s 2026 State of Agentic AI Adoption, Volume III, the lowest-capability models averaged 501 on decision override, a 0 to 1,000 score, while the most capable models averaged 45, a gap of more than 10x. Roughly a third of the scored model references in US environments fall in that lowest group. Governing them starts with a live inventory of the AI estate, including which models are in play, and policies that apply before an agent acts.

Why this evaluation matters

In our view, Forrester's evaluation reflects these shifts in operating model, and it assessed agentic development security across the full span of AI-driven development: the code agents produce, the agents and the components they pull in, and the AI applications teams build. Forrester asks buyers to weigh three considerations:

Visibility and governance of agentic development

Verification of AI-generated code and AI applications

AI risk reduction at agentic speed

Teams now need coverage across all three, on one platform that shares context between them, and that is the standard we have been building toward.

A decade of conviction, pointed at where software is created now

Snyk has operated on a core belief for more than a decade: security belongs where software is created. We believe agentic development moves that point of creation inside the agent workflow, and that is where the Snyk AI Security Platform is built to operate. Forrester’s report states that "Snyk articulates a farsighted vision to secure AI-written code, the agents that run it, and the applications they build, while advancing secure-at-inception development and governance."

On capabilities, the report states that "Snyk brings security into developer and AI coding agent workflows through autofix and coding guardrails that secure AI- and human-generated code and block risky agent actions." It also notes that Snyk's "strong AI dynamic testing uncovers business logic flaws and vulnerability chains and validates findings with working exploits."

How Evo by Snyk secures each layer of AI-driven development

Last year, Snyk expanded the Snyk AI Security Platform with Evo by Snyk, a suite of agent-native security solutions that secure, protect, and govern AI-driven development across three loops: the code artifact, the AI workforce, and the AI applications teams build. A validation layer tests all three.

Evo Agentic AppSec: Secure the code artifact. AI security agents that find, fix, and block vulnerabilities at the speed agents write code, with every result verified independently. This includes Snyk Secrets for blocking leaked credentials.

Evo Agentic Development Security (ADS): Protect the AI workforce. Governs what AI coding agents use, what they do, and what they generate, from the MCP servers and skills they pull in to the code they write. This includes Snyk Studio for real-time guidance in AI coding workflows.

Evo AI-SPM: Govern every AI app you build. Discovers and assesses risk of the models, agents, skills, and MCP servers in your software, generates a live AI-BOM, and turns AI policy into enforceable controls.

Evo Continuous Offensive Security (COS): Validate every loop. Continuously tests applications and AI agents, leveraging Agent Red Teaming, and returns validated proof of what an attacker could actually exploit, so no loop grades its own work.

As AI takes on more of the work of building software, we believe its output needs a separate, deterministic layer to verify it. That is why Snyk pairs frontier AI reasoning with our deterministic engines and ten years of security intelligence, so organizations can adopt AI at full speed and stay accountable for what they ship.

What this means for teams building with AI agents

Forrester's take: "Snyk is a good fit for enterprises that want to accelerate agentic development while embedding security directly into agent workflows." For teams evaluating this market, three questions help separate tools built for agentic development from tools adapted to it:

Governance: Can you see and control what your agents use, what they do, and what they generate before it ships?

Remediation: Is your fix rate keeping pace with your rate of new risk, across new code and the existing backlog?

Proof: What independent evidence shows your controls hold against a real attacker?

We are grateful to our customers, partners, and the developer community, whose feedback shapes the platform every day. We will keep investing inside the agent loop, where software is now created. Our mission remains the same: unleash AI innovators, securely.

Title: PHP2Shell Won't Be the Last. Here's Where the Next One Will Show Up First.
Context: The first question every team faced was where PHP was answering requests, and whether someone could exploit it right then and there
Full Text:
On October 17, Amazon's honeypot network logged a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt from an anonymized IP address. Yet, public disclosure was still four days away.

By the time PHP got its fixes in on October 21, the technical details had already leaked, proof-of-concept exploits were in wide circulation, and more exploit attempts were being logged left and right. The issue was that there were two critical, unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in the PHP engine itself (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both CVSS v4.0 9.2) -- what we now know as PHP2Shell.

Our own Security Research team covered what happened and what you should do: which releases to move to, which mitigations you could put in place to reduce exposure until you were able to update, and where each part of the Snyk platform sees the problem.

This post now picks up where our Security Research team left off. We want to talk about what the response taught us: where this kind of exposure lives and comes from, why answering fast depends on the work we’d done months earlier, and why the next one is already on its way.

Why was PHP2Shell a problem for teams with clean code?

Well, because the vulnerabilities live below the code. And what does that mean? Both of the mentioned CVEs happen in the request lifecycle of the PHP engine, which makes them reachable before any application code actually runs. On Apache, with mod_php, an exploit needed but a single unauthenticated request.

Now, think about that for a second. You probably had careful reviews, clean code, plus a neat and tidy dependency tree, all sitting above the actual problem. The first question every team faced was where PHP was answering requests, and whether someone could exploit it right then and there.

The question was about running applications. The very same question attackers will always start with.

Which inventory tells you where PHP is running?

Each type of inventory tells you part of it.

PHP reaches production via a Dockerfile, a distribution package, a platform image, or manually. A "php": ">=8.2"constraint in composer.json tells you what an application accepts, and then the deployed version depends on which of those routes installed it. Container scans see PHP installed from distribution packages once each distribution publishes its advisory, and PHP compiled from source, including the official PHP Docker images, falls outside that view. (Once again, our research team's post maps exactly which Snyk view sees which slice of this reality.)

Then there's the version string. VirusTotal fingerprints roughly 5.1 million IP addresses running PHP, and only about 1.1 million of them announce a version, so roughly four out of five hide it. Their summary is one of the cleanest lines we've read on the subject anywhere: "If you only search for a version string, you only see the fraction of the problem that volunteers it."

The gap between what your inside-out views know and what actually answers from the outside is where the real risk lies. Attackers hit your URL, and PHP2Shell is the purest case of that we’ve seen. Anyone probing for it ends up asking the same question: Does PHP answer on this URL?

What did the response look like from the outside in?

The head start: before PHP's 14:00 UTC release on October 21, Snyk had advisories live for both CVEs, so monitored projects would get a hit the moment fixed versions were known. Within about 30 minutes of the release, those advisories included affected ranges and fixed versions, and distribution advisories followed as each distribution was published. That covered what Snyk Container and Unmanaged scans could tell you.

Three questions ran through Snyk API & Web:

Where is PHP running? Discovery enumerates the assets on your domains and fingerprints their technology stack. Set the Tech filter to PHP, and you get every discovered host and endpoint where PHP was identified, with its risk rating, score, and last-seen date. Version numbers come later, from the hosts themselves. As our research team put it, before you can patch, you need the list.

Can someone exploit it? Within 24 hours of PHP's release, the full scan profile tested for PHP2Shell, and teams could run that check on their own as a custom profile for a fast answer across every PHP target.

Did the fix hold? Run the same custom profile after patching, and pair it with your distribution's advisory or patch level, because a patched distribution build can keep an older version number.

So, Discovery --> targeted check --> patch --> re-test: probe, observe, and infer, against a clock that now runs in hours. And that’s exactly the most concerning part, what we care about the most. For teams already running Snyk API & Web, the hard part was done before October 21: their domains were mapped, and their applications set up as targets. When the check was there, the response took only a filter and a quick scan.

For us, that’s one of the main returns on having continuous outside-in testing: the work that answers at day one gets done months before that.

If PHP2Shell is detectable from the outside, what was the hard part?

Time.

In May, we laid out the distinction on which COS is built. Heuristic-detectable vulnerabilities show themselves to deterministic tools: throw payloads at a running application or API, observe the responses, and infer. Context-dependent vulnerabilities (BOLA, cross-tenant leakage, and chained business logic) carry no signature at all, because they live in the gap between what an application is supposed to do and what it actually does.

Once it was known, PHP2Shell became testable from the outside, which puts it squarely in that first class of heuristic-detectable vulns. The hard part, the constraint, was the gap between a disclosure and having a check running against everything you expose. That gap is the attacker’s window to exploit, and this time it opened four days before disclosure eventually did.

The disclosure kept moving, too. On October 23, the PHP project described a partial bypass (CVE-2026-115560) that applies when an application switches its session serialization handler with ini_set() before starting the session, with upload progress enabled. Its preconditions are rare, and whatever you concluded on Wednesday still needed a second look by Friday. A point-in-time answer ages in days.

Why won't PHP2Shell be the last?

There are three reasons for that. Due to the nature of how they were found:

Because they were found with AI assistance, in an engine that has served the web for three decades. Our research team put it plainly: "In a world of LLMs and agents, everybody is still running servers." And the kind of model that found these vulnerabilities is the kind attackers now have in their hands.

The stronger cadence. Manoj Nair, Snyk's CTO and Chief Innovation Officer, described it in September: "The kind of severe flaw that AI now surfaces in widely used software, the sort of find that used to arrive once or twice a year and reset everyone's quarter, is landing several times a week in what I'm seeing."

The much faster clock. CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, drew two lessons from PHP2Shell that apply well beyond it. Defenders "should not assume the public disclosure date is the earliest date of exploitation." And "the time from patch to working exploit is shrinking for structural reasons," because AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or an advisory into a working exploit. His advice for critical vulnerabilities in internet-facing systems: "measure patch and mitigation timelines in hours."

What does being ready for the next one take?

Strip out the product names, and it comes down to four properties. Judge any approach by them (ours included). Don’t think about product names, but how it all comes down to four properties. And you should judge any approach with these (ours included!)

An inventory that exists before the advisory does. Built from the outside in and kept current, so a new disclosure starts with a filter.

Checks that ship in hours. The gap between an advisory and a running test is the attacker's window. Measure it.

Re-tests on demand. The same targeted check, run again until the fix holds.

Testing that needs no signature. Heuristics catch what someone has already described. Everything else takes reasoning: testing that works out what your application is supposed to do, then goes after the gap between that and what it actually does.

As for Snyk, here’s how that maps to what we offer.

Snyk API & Web carries the first three: Discovery, an engine the team keeps current as disclosures land, and targeted profiles you can run and re-run. Continuous Offensive Security adds the fourth: AI Pentesting reasons about your application the way a pentester would, Agent Red Teaming engages the moment recon spots an LLM in the stack, and Dynamic Testing, the Snyk API & Web engine, covers the heuristic classes underneath, continuously. In our platform's terms, that's Validate: continuously attack your applications to prove fixes held and show what's still exploitable.

Then there's posture. At The AI Security Panel: Unfiltered on October 14, Manoj asked the question we keep coming back to: "When an autonomous attacker is going to attack you, why don't you attack yourself?" That question is the whole premise of COS. On our side, the work is shrinking every single gap in this story: from advisory to running check, and from check to confirmed fix.

Which engine, and when, is anyone's guess now. Where it shows up first is easier to call: at your URL. That's where your testing should already be.

Title: Snyk UNFILTERED: Inside Our First-Ever Customer Summit
Context: Finding vulnerabilities is only half the job Detection is no longer the bottleneck
Full Text:
What happens when you bring security leaders from some of the world's most forward-thinking organizations into one room, close the doors, and invite them to speak candidly about what's working, what's breaking, and what they’re still working out?

That’s what we set out to find with Snyk UNFILTERED, our inaugural Customer Summit. Held in San Francisco ahead of the launch of Evo Agentic AppSec and the AI Security Summit, Snyk UNFILTERED was designed to feel nothing like a conference.

We brought together a small group of security leaders from our customer community for an afternoon of candid discussions, interactive debates, and peer-to-peer exchanges. With no traditional presentations, product demos, or carefully rehearsed talking points, the summit gave attendees the freedom to share their experiences without attribution. What followed was an open exchange of ideas about the challenges and opportunities shaping the future of AI security. Leaders compared notes on real rollouts, real roadblocks, and real questions they have not yet figured out, with a level of transparency that is hard to find at traditional industry events.

From the growing backlog of vulnerabilities to the governance of autonomous agents, attendees challenged assumptions, compared real-world experiences, and explored questions the industry is still answering. And that's where the most valuable conversations began.

Five key takeaways that stuck with us

Five themes kept resurfacing over the afternoon, across every table and every discussion:

1. When AI writes the code, who owns the risk?

If an engineer prompts an AI tool to build an agent skill and that skill causes an issue later, who is at fault? The room kept coming back to the importance of guardrails: clear controls and ownership that hold up even when no human typed the line.

2. The AI conversation has grown up

Just a few months ago, the questions were about cost and token usage. Now leadership wants to know the return on investment, what AI is really costing, and where to set budget caps. AI has moved from experiment to line item with scrutiny to match.

3. Finding vulnerabilities is only half the job

Detection is no longer the bottleneck. The questions have moved to how teams fix issues, how fast they can fix them, and how they reduce human error within the loop. Fixes that stall in review, testing, and merge were a shared frustration.

4. Risk can come from anywhere

When everyone on a team has access to AI, vulnerabilities can come from anywhere. Democratizing AI also spreads responsibility, and attendees talked about how to keep everyone accountable without slowing anyone down.

5. Humans can only do so much

Teams are limited by how much people can review and approve. Leaders are open to trusting agents, but only with controls that an agent cannot bypass, and with governance designed for machines rather than adapted from processes built for people.

From UNFILTERED conversations to the future of AI Security

Snyk UNFILTERED was just the beginning of an important week in San Francisco. The challenges discussed behind closed doors at UNFILTERED reflected a broader shift happening across the industry: security teams are moving beyond simply identifying risk toward enabling organizations to build, innovate, and operate safely at AI speed.

The next morning, we launched Evo Agentic AppSec, and the AI Security Summit brought builders, researchers, investors, and CISOs into the same building. The questions from the customer room about fixing at speed and governing agents were carried straight into those conversations. Hearing those challenges directly from customers shapes what we build next.

The best conversations don't end when the event does

The leaders in the room are navigating enormous change. They’re balancing innovation with accountability and securing technologies that evolve faster than the processes designed to govern them. What made the afternoon valuable was their willingness to talk openly about what they haven’t solved yet. Spaces like that are rare, and we plan to keep creating them.

Snyk Unfiltered is part of our commitment to bringing our customer community together through candid conversations and shared learning, and this was the first of many.

Title: PHP Patches Two Critical Unauthenticated RCEs (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619): [Updated for CVE-2026-115560]
Context: In a world of LLMs and agents, everybody is still running servers - and the model that found these is the same kind of model attackers now have, which is the premise behind Evo...
Full Text:
On Wednesday, October 21, 2026 at 14:00 UTC, the PHP project released PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 to fix two critical vulnerabilities, both rated CVSS v4.0 9.2, that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. The PHP security team advises: "There are no complete mitigations; updating is the only safe choice."

These are bugs in the PHP runtime, not in a Composer package. That changes how you detect and fix them, as we explain below

TL;DR If you run PHP that serves web requests (PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed), update to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35 today. If you are on 8.1 or older, get a backported package from your distribution or LTS vendor, or upgrade.

What happened

Times are in UTC.

October 20: The PHP security team published an advance notice of a critical security release scheduled for October 21 at 14:00 UTC. It fixes two vulnerabilities assessed as CVSS v4.0 9.2, with the right reserved to release early if details leak or exploitation is seen in the wild.

October 21, before 14:00 UTC: Snyk published advisories for both CVEs, SNYK-UNMANAGED-PHP-21347795 (CVE-2026-109618) and SNYK-UNMANAGED-PHP-21347796 (CVE-2026-109619), to alert customers to the action they will need to take and so that monitored projects get a hit the moment the fixed versions are known.

October 21, 14:00 UTC: The PHP security advisory and the four fixed releases go live. Within about 30 minutes, Snyk's advisories are updated with all relevant details, including affected ranges and fixed versions.

October 21 onward: Linux distributions (which received the patches in advance) start publishing their own advisories. Snyk publishes advisories for them as they appear, for example SNYK-UBUNTU2604-PHP85-21373920. The running list is at CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

Update @ October 23: keep session.upload_progress.enabled=0

On October 23, the PHP project published an informational advisory for CVE-2026-115560, a CVE that is reserved but not yet assigned. It describes a partial bypass vector for CVE-2026-109619. The setting that prevents it, session.upload_progress.enabled=0, was already listed as a mitigation for CVE-2026-109619.

PHP is not rushing an emergency fix because the preconditions for exploitation are rare and unlikely to apply to most deployments. An application must configure session.serialize_handler as php_binary or php_serialize, then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(), while session upload progress is enabled. Applications that never change the serialization handler at runtime can keep the feature on.

The vulnerabilities

Both are in the request lifecycle of the PHP engine, making them reachable before any application code runs. This is one factor that makes these vulnerabilities both widespread and dangerous.

Technical details

CVE-2026-109618, RCE via out-of-memory corruption: Out-of-memory handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup, then treats the invalid data as valid. An attacker who can drive a worker to its memory limit with a malicious request can trigger the interrupt.

CVE-2026-109619, RCE via stale global state: Request-owned internal state can survive after its backing memory has been freed. A later request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before normal initialization resets it. In a long-lived worker model that comprises a cross-request use-after-free.

These bugs were found with AI assistance, in a runtime that has been in production for three decades. In a world of LLMs and agents, everybody is still running servers - and the model that found these is the same kind of model attackers now have, which is the premise behind Evo by Snyk: AI-driven security for the applications that agents run on, not only for the agents themselves. AI-assisted discovery is also why PHP2Shell won’t be the last flaw of its kind, and why response timelines are now measured in hours.

Who is affected

All PHP installations serving web requests are at risk. That covers PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed, etc. Apache with mod_php is most vulnerable, with a demonstrated exploit in which a single unauthenticated request triggers the attack before application code runs.

PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project, so an unpatched 8.1, 8.0, or 7.4 install is affected with no upstream fix. Given the severity, the PHP security team did publish minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 for people who build from source or have no LTS vendor.

What you should do now

Update. Fixed versions are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. Note that 8.2 reaches end of life on December 31, 2026, so if you are on 8.2, this is also your cue to plan the next bump.

Check your vendor. Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches ahead of release. Pull their updated packages rather than waiting for a source build. A patched distro build can keep an older version number, so check the distro’s advisory or patch level too.

Verify what’s actually running. Check the PHP version on each host and image (php -v or the image tag). Scan results alone can’t confirm that an installation is fixed.

If you cannot update today, PHP lists mitigations that reduce exposure to specific paths without making an install safe: memory_limit=-1 set where applications cannot override it, a low post_max_size, session.upload_progress.enabled=0 followed by a restart of every worker, and on 8.5 fatal_error_backtraces=0. See the relevant advisory for the caveats on each.

Whether or not you have updated, keep session.upload_progress.enabled=0 set until the next regular bugfix release if your application switches session.serialize_handler at runtime. See the update above for details.

On PHP 8.1 or older, upgrade to a supported version or get a backported package from your distribution or LTS vendor. PHP’s source backports for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 are a last resort for teams building from source.

The open source side

The PHP security team gave the ecosystem a day's notice with a fixed time, a severity, and no exploitation details. They pre-shared patches with Linux distributions so packaged fixes could be released alongside the source release. They published backports for unsupported versions (7.4, 8.0, 8.1). They told users of a popular volunteer repo (rpms.remirepo.net) that it would not be updated on day one and what to do instead. And their mitigation guidance is very transparent about what each setting does not protect against.

That is what coordinated disclosure looks like when a volunteer-run project does it right. It is also why, at Snyk, we were able to have advisories live before the release and complete shortly after it: a published schedule lets everyone downstream prepare.

Snyk SCA Behavior

Snyk Open Source reads what your application declares in manifest or build files, like composer.json, composer.lock. The PHP interpreter is not a declared dependency. It is installed by a Dockerfile, a distribution package, a platform image, or by hand. A "php": ">=8.2" constraint in composer.json tells you what the application accepts, but not precisely what is deployed.

How the Snyk Platform helps you find exposed PHP

What you use

What you will see for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619

Snyk Open Source (CLI or SCM integration)

The CVEs themselves are not reported because the PHP runtime is not a regular dependency in your manifest file. For PHP/Composer projects, Snyk shows the application's declared dependencies, which can help you identify which of your projects are PHP applications. The declared PHP version constraint does not tell you which version is deployed.

Snyk C/C++ Unmanaged scanning

Advisories are reported when the PHP runtime is present in your project, and can be filtered by CVE ID.

Snyk Container

PHP installed from Linux distribution packages is reported once the distribution has published its advisory. Some supported distributions have published advisories, which are available in test results (for example, SNYK-RHEL10-PHP84-21392647 and SNYK-UBUNTU2604-PHP85-21373920). We are importing others as they publish, which are available here: CVE-2026-109618 CVE-2026-109619. PHP compiled from source, including the official php: Docker images, is not detected by Snyk Container.

Snyk API & Web

DAST examines and tests running applications from the outside and fingerprints their technology stack. If a customer's application is exposed to php2shell, we detect and report it

Zero Day report

The Snyk Zero Day report matches your projects to the advisories, so it can only list projects scanned using “Unmanaged scans” or Container scans of distribution packages. For Open Source-only projects, it will show no results.

Finding your PHP attack surface with Snyk API & Web

Before you can patch, you need the list. Snyk API & Web's Discovery tab enumerates assets found on your domains and fingerprints their technology stack. Open Discovery, set the Tech filter to PHP, and you have every discovered host and endpoint where PHP was identified, with its risk rating, score, and last-seen date, ready to scan or add as a target.

The same Tech filter is also available in the Targets list, so the applications you added can be narrowed to PHP the same way.

This does not tell you the PHP version. It tells you where to look, which is a crucial step towards remediation.

Test against the vulnerability with Snyk API & Web

Snyk API & Web allows you to scan your applications and APIs and detect if you are vulnerable to the PHP2Shell vulnerability.

A scan with a full profile now tests for the PHP2Shell vulnerability. Additionally, you can create a custom scan profile that tests against PHP2Shell exclusively, ensuring you have a quick way to know if your applications are vulnerable or if your remediation has taken place already.

What we are doing

Advisories for both CVEs were published before PHP's 14:00 UTC release and updated with affected versions and fix details within about 30 minutes of it.

An additional advisory has been published for CVE-2026-115560, which will be updated as details and the fix for it are released.

Distribution advisories are being imported as each Linux distribution publishes. Ubuntu and Red Hat are available now.

A Zero Day report for this event is available for Unmanaged and Container projects.

As always, Snyk's security research team is tracking this disclosure and will update the advisories as new information arrives. If you have questions, contact your Snyk account team or Support.

Title: Turn Your Vulnerability Backlog Into Pull Requests With Agentic Remediation
Context: For example, an AppSec team can launch a campaign targeting high- and critical-severity dependency vulnerabilities across repositories in a Snyk Organization
Full Text:
The Evo Remediation Agent is now in Open Preview, bringing automated dependency resolution to Evo Agentic AppSec. AppSec teams can now run ongoing remediation campaigns across repositories and deliver proposed fixes to developers through validated pull requests.

Fixing a dependency vulnerability can mean choosing an upgrade, resolving dependency conflicts, adapting the application, and/or checking the result. That work competes with everything developers are already building. As teams introduce code and new vulnerabilities at increasingly exponential rates, AppSec needs a way to accelerate remediation across the applications they protect.

With the help of agentic remediation, AppSec teams can start by leveraging campaigns targeting a defined set of repositories and vulnerabilities. Snyk supplies the model and hosted sandbox environment, and developers receive proposed changes through their existing source code management (SCM) workflow. The developers continue to retain control over final review and merging.

Give AppSec a way to drive fixes

A remediation campaign defines which vulnerabilities the agent works on, in which repositories, and on what schedule. AppSec teams set the scope, and Evo Remediation Agent works through eligible vulnerabilities and opens pull requests for developers to review.

For example, an AppSec team can launch a campaign targeting high- and critical-severity dependency vulnerabilities across repositories in a Snyk Organization. Recurring campaigns repeat that work on a schedule as repositories and vulnerability findings change.

That gives AppSec teams a way to initiate remediation without asking each developer to install and run an agent. Teams can follow repository outcomes across a campaign, review where the agent produced fixes, and investigate where remediation efforts still need attention.

Snyk first brought automated dependency updates into developer workflows with automatic Fix PRs across SCA and Container. Agent Fix extended remediation to source-code vulnerabilities detected by Snyk Code, our first AI-native solution generating and checking proposed fixes. The initial Evo Remediation Agent then brought a broader workflow into the CLI and ADE: plan the fix, apply changes, and validate the result in the developer’s environment. Now, fully validated, the next iteration of the Evo Remediation Agent brings campaigns that automate agentic remediation to AppSec teams.

Starting once again with Open Source vulnerabilities, teams can put the agent to work across repositories and make remediation an ongoing part of their security program.

Security context guides the work

A dependency update can require changes throughout an application. The agent uses Snyk findings to plan updates, applies changes in a hosted sandbox, and checks its work with builds, available tests, and rescans. This feedback helps the agent work through the changes an upgrade requires.

When the agent produces a fix, it opens a pull request and records each action attached to the change. Teams can restrict campaigns to fixes assessed as non-breaking, and the agent does not merge changes. Developers review the proposed changes and decide whether to merge them.

Evidence behind the remediation engine

Generating a fix only helps reduce risk if a developer can merge it. A pull request that breaks the build, fails existing tests, or leaves the vulnerability in place adds review work and doesn’t shrink the backlog. A high mergeable fix rate is what turns agent fix suggestions into backlog reduction because more of the fix pull requests actually get merged with less developer rework.

The VulnBump benchmark tests the mergeable fix rate of the engine that powers Evo Remediation Agent. Across 307 dependency-upgrade tasks, the CLI-based Remediation Agent passed all four verification checks on 90.2% of tasks. Claude Code with Snyk findings passed 77.5%, and Claude Code alone passed 59.6%. All three used the same model.

Those checks cover the outcomes that matter to a dependency fix: dependencies resolve, the targeted vulnerabilities disappear on rescan, the application builds, and previously passing tests still pass. The results show the value of combining security context with a purpose-built remediation workflow.

Fix first. Prioritize the rest.

Remediation programs usually start by deciding what to fix. Evo Remediation Agent reverses that order, giving AppSec teams another way to act on the backlog. Recurring campaigns work through eligible vulnerabilities in scope, so what reaches your team is then the work that needs human judgment.

Repository outcomes and journals help teams understand where the agent made progress and where further work remains. AppSec teams get a running view not only of the backlog, but also the pull requests opened, while developers get a record of why each change was made. Remediation consequently becomes an ongoing part of the security program, with your team setting the standard for what ships.

Bring remediation to your team

Workspaces
